speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: BANKRUPTCIES-ASTRA TRUST-RE-MOR-INQUIRY WHETHER CIRCUMSTANCES WILL BE EXAMINED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 10 last, I asked some questions concerning the bankruptcy of Re-Mor Investment Management and Astra Trust. I called for a judicial inquiry. I want to add a few more details now, as much as the time allotted to me will allow.
The liquidation of Astra Trust, the bankruptcy of Re-Mor Investment Management and the receivership of C & M Financial Consultants are three events that are interconnected through common ownership of share stock, common directors, and twisted, crooked business dealings designed at the outset to bilk innocent victims of their life savings.
Not only are the depositors of Astra Trust victims, but some of the shareholders have been gutted by a group of financial sharks who have left behind a trail of shattered lives, broken dreams, threats of suicide out of despair, and a cynicism so deep that it could lead to violence.
The victims of the Re-Mor scam were baited by the smooth talking trust officers who took their money, gave Astra Trust receipts to the victims, and then switched the money to worthless Re-Mor mortgages. When the victims complained they were told they were holders of good solid first mortgages, when, in reality, they own a piece of a fourth or fifth mortgage that is next to worthless.
The purists in business practice cannot invoke caveat emp-tor-"Let the buyer beware"-because most of the innocent victims entered the door of a trust company that, on its walls, windows and counters, displayed the advice that Astra Trust was a member of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. You see, they had that feeling-a warm comfortable feeling, that the government was there to protect them. Add into this mixture of deception, that the words "guarantee" and "guaranteed" were prominently displayed in the office, in advertising wall charts and brochures, and so on; add as well that Astra was paying a slightly higher rate of interest than other trust companies and you then begin to see the dimension of the scam. A trust company-protection by a government corporation and guaranteed; that is the perceived picture of the innocent victims who walked into this place.
Adjournment Debate
But, as in most deceptive dealings, there was another side that was not up front or displayed. This was the fact that the trust officers were also commission agents for Re-Mor. They were paid a salary by Astra and a commission by Re-Mor. They took the money from their "mark" in a trust-govern-ment-protected-guaranteed atmosphere and switched the money to Remor worthless mortgages.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bus-sieres) has tried to weasel out of a dirty, smelly, disgusting mess by saying that Re-Mor is a provincial responsibility. Mr. Speaker, bankruptcy is a federal responsibility and Re-Mor Investment Management Corporation is bankrupt.
There are dozens of unanswered questions that must be investigated. Let me list a few. Is the Department of Insurance adequately staffed and does it have the mandate to perform an adequate inspection of the trust industry? After all, it was only a short time ago that Argosy Trust left behind a trail of shattered certificate holders. How close were the affairs of Astra Trust monitored by the Department of Insurance? What liaison is there between the federal and provincial governments? I am sure we could write volumes about that. What leverage does the Department of Insurance have that it can get the Ontario Securities Commission to hold back on a "stop trading" order on a trust company that has violated the regulations under which it operates? Did the inspectors from the Department of Insurance put the advertising of Astra Trust to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs when it is obvious that the advertising is misleading? Why did the Department of Insurance not intervene when it was apparent that the trust officers in Astra Trust were acting as commission agents for Re-Mor? Surely they saw the conflict. Surely they knew the amount of money that was passing through Astra Trust and where it came from.
If, when the trust licence was given to Astra Trust, the government instructed Astra Trust to close down C & M Financial Services, why did it act blind to the activities of Re-Mor when it knew C & M really never closed down?
Did the Department of Insurance inspector's report to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs indicate that bait and switch tactics were being used by Astra Trust officers? Why did they not do it then? Certainly they were there and had enough evidence to work on.
What liaison was there between the Department of Insurance and CMHC when that agency listed Re-Mor as an approved lender? How much money was diverted from Astra Trust to a condominium development in Spain? How many million, and do we really know if it went to that development or is it in a numbered bank account in Switzerland or Liechen-stein? RCMP officials traced the money as far as they could, but were the directors of Astra Trust that inept that they would invest trust funds in a venture that was so questionable? Or was it chosen as a front to divert money to a hidden account that could be retrieved at a later date?

January 12, 1981
Adjournment Debate
With a mass of regulatory violations outstanding against Astra Trust after 12 months of operation, why was no firm action taken at that time before the whole mess festered and grew into the tangled fraud we see today?
I could go on, but in the final analysis the bankruptcy of Re-Mor and the liquidation of Astra Trust is a scar on the whole trust industry, and that industry, while some expressed their view verbally regarding the licensing of Astra Trust, not one of them put it in writing. Nor did their trade association put in writing their concerns of the licensing of Astra to the Department of Insurance or the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
So, we must ask, whom do you trust? To whom do unsophisticated investors turn when they wish to invest the proceeds of the sale of their home or a bequest or other funds they have available?
We must have a wide open judicial inquiry, if necessary a joint federal and provincial inquiry. The personal assets of the officers and directors of Astra, Re-Mor and C & M should be frozen. The assets of their wives should be frozen so that the inquiry can determine if loans and other funds have been diverted or transferred to second or third persons to shield them from seizure as the result of the liquidation, bankruptcy and receivership of the tangled companies involved.
If you fail to do this, then you are confirming that you condone and are part of this mammoth conspiracy and the word trust, as we understand it today, will cease to have any meaning in financial dealings.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BANKRUPTCIES-ASTRA TRUST-RE-MOR-INQUIRY WHETHER CIRCUMSTANCES WILL BE EXAMINED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to try to answer some of the charges or points raised by the hon. member with regard to Astra Trust. 1 would first like to put a little background on the record.
The Astra Trust Company was authorized to commence business in early 1977. The deposit activities of the company were generally carried out in a satisfactory way, but a problem arose through the course of 1978 in connection with a pooled trust fund operated by the company, known as the Agency Trust Fund. The documentation was inadequate and the investments were not of acceptable quality.
The Department of Insurance communicated with the Registrar of Trust Companies in Ontario and with the Ontario Securities Commission to try to solve the problem with company management. Further intake of funds through the Agency Trust Fund was prohibited.
The difficulty was apparently solved in the fall of 1978 by an agreement whereby the three principal shareholders would purchase certain assets out of the Agency Trust Fund, paying in instalments.
In the spring of 1979, it appeared that Mr. Montemurro, the president of Astra Trust, secured the incorporation of a company called Re-Mor Investment Management Corporation under the Ontario law and had it licensed as a mortgage broker. We received no information concerning this incorporation but would not normally by informed of the issuance of a mortgage broker's licence. No one supervised this company.
In the spring of 1980, the Ontario Securities Commission took action to investigate the activities of Re-Mor. It then appeared that the assets of Re-Mor were of poor quality and the company was put in bankruptcy. The Department of Insurance then learned of the existence of this company and that the company's obligations had been sold out of the branches of Astra, often being presented as insured obligations.
In Astra, problems relating to the Agency Trust Fund re-emerged at the end of 1979. In early 1980, no solution was in sight and the company's licence was severely restricted. These problems, together with potential claims arising from the Re-Mor bankruptcy, uncertainty of management and allegations of fraudulent activity by the principal shareholders of Astra led the Department of Insurance to seize control of the company's assets in April and later to seek a winding up order.
Astra Trust is now in the process of being liquidated. Practically all of the insured deposits have been paid off by funds advanced by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
Uncertainty continues respecting creditors of Re-Mor. Re-Mor is an Ontario company and is not a trust company. It is not a member of the CDIC. The matter is very complex and studies are under way to disclose the complete details of any involvements between Re-Mor and Astra. Solicitors representing the CDIC, the liquidator of Astra and the trustee in bankruptcy of Re-Mor, are working together in this investigation.
The Department of Insurance and the CDIC have requested the RCMP to press forward adequate investigations to reveal fraudulent or other criminal activities that may have been involved. The Ontario Provincial Police are also active in this regard.
Everyone may be assured that all lines of investigation are being pursued with a view to doing everything possible to minimize losses to creditors and to see that justice is done.
If I could, on two points, the hon. member opposite has indicated that the federal government-

FISHERIES-INQUIRY WHETHER CATCH ROYALTY OR LANDING TAX WILL BE IMPOSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of this Thirty-second Parliament, the government promised as recorded in the Speech from the Throne at page 6 of Hansard that-legislation will be introduced to guarantee adequate investment in the fishing sector through partial cost recovery and reinvestment of enhanced earnings.
On May 8, 1980, arising out of that reference in the Speech from the Throne, 1 addressed questions to the hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) seeking further clarification of this reference in the throne speech which implied that another form of supplementary tax would be imposed upon the west coast fishermen of Canada in particular. This tax, sometimes referred to as a resource rent or a landing charge, would be used perhaps-although the minister has not made it clear-to finance the cost of the salmon enhancement program, primarily focusing on the Fraser River and other coastal waters. But as far as my understanding of the attitude within the fisheries department is concerned, this tax might also be used to finance the general management expenses of the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
The west coast fishing industry is worth some $300 million annually, at least it was up until last year, which was a very poor year, and the administration of that fishery by the officials in British Columbia is costing some $35 million a year or one-tenth of the landed value of the catch.
It is common knowledge that the officials within the Department of Fisheries and Oceans have been contemplating the imposition of this form of income tax surcharge for several years. They have been thinking about a tax in the magnitude of 10 per cent of the value of the fish caught. If the value of the landed fish is in the order of $300 million, it would suggest a windfall tax to the government of some $30 million, which almost equals the total operating budget of the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans on the Pacific coast.
It is a common attitude within the Department of Fisheries to consider that fishermen are making windfall profits-that is the language used by some officials of that department-and that we need to generate more revenue to manage the resource by skimming off some of these windfall profits which would presumably result from the Salmonid Enhancement Program and rising fish prices. The minister ought to try telling that to a west coast fisherman these days. I have information that in the recent weeks, as a consequence of ineffective management policies of the federal department and collapsing price structures worldwide, there have been 62 bankruptcies or near bankruptcies of vessel owners on the Pacific coast registered with the Royal Bank alone.
The whole notion of a landings tax is predicated on the concept that there is some cushion or some windfall profit which is just ripe to be skimmed off by government bureaucrats. They like any program which will enable them to do that, even if it means the average little guy out there in his gill
Adjournment Debate
net boat or troller will be faced with virtual bankruptcy when he comes to shore because of the impact of that tax.
The notion of a resource rent or landing tax was first proposed by a gentleman named Sol Sinclair, who was retained by the federal government almost four years ago to come up with certains options for improving the management of the west coast fishery. From three options, the option of controlling and regulating the resource through licensing, controlling it through quotas or controlling it by establishing a tax charged against the value of the resource, Mr. Sinclair proposed that the landings tax or royalty approach be developed.
That has been the guiding light and the guiding star for the Department of Fisheries and Oceans ever since in holding the idea of this tax over the heads of the fishermen but not really coming down to talking about how big this tax would be, how the revenues would be used and to what extent the fishermen themselves would have some say in the spending of those revenues and the investing of those revenues in their own best interests through some board of trustees and through the deposit of these funds in some clearly identified trust account. It is common knowledge that government departments fear and are very reluctant to contemplate the establishment of special trust accounts for special purposes. They would prefer to throw money, taxes and surtaxes into general revenues and then spend them as they see best fit. In this case such an approach to the administration of such a landings tax would be very improper and unacceptable to the fishermen.
Those who have taken the time to read his report will know that Mr. Sinclair did a survey of fishermen, and this is recorded in the appendix to the Sol Sinclair report. He found that a majority of fishermen oppose the notion of implementing a landings tax to finance even the Salmonid Enhancement Program.
In a random sample of some 33 fishermen only 11 favoured a royalty and some 19 opposed the imposition of a catch royalty. In addition, many fishermen argued as follows, and I am quoting from a statement by a spokesman for the Prince Rupert Fish Exchange:
It can also be argued that salmon enhancement will benefit.all Canadians by increased general taxation, creating more employment and in general improving the economic situation in Canada. Many government subsidized plans have been put into effect in the prairies for the farmers and the east coast for the fisheries. We do not know of any pay back or cost sharing and would think that expecting a cost recovery from the enhancement plan is a bit unfair.
It is the general view of fishermen on the west coast that this tax is very unfair.

A condition of the federal government's approval for the Pacific Salmonid Enhancement Program was the government's investment in this program could be subject to cost recovery.
In March, 1979, an agreement on the SEP was signed with the province of British Columbia in which both parties agreed on the principle of cost recovery by the federal government through licence fees from marine fisheries and landings charges on commercial fish landings.
Following the signing of this agreement the Department of Fisheries and Oceans began an analysis of how and when such a program could be implemented. The subject of landings charges has been discussed with all interested groups participating in Pacific coast fisheries as well as with the government of British Columbia.
On October 28, 1980, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) announced in Vancouver, B.C. that, and I quote:
Due to the poor fishing year in 1980. and the absence of necessary legislation, a plan to introduce landings charges on commercially-caught salmon will be delayed. A scheme will be reached for implementation in 1982 in the hope that 1981 will bring higher salmon catches and better prices than this year.
The rate of landings charges has not yet been determined.
The legislative authority for such a program is being examined; however, currently there are no plans as to when such legislation will be introduced.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-U.S. FIGHTER AIRCRAFT CRASHING ON CANADIAN SOIL
NATIONAL DEFENCE-U.S. FIGHTER AIRCRAFT CRASHING ON CANADIAN SOIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address myself to a question which I put quite some time ago. In fact I raised this question in the House in the summer during the heavy fire season in western Canada and in Ontario. Until the end of the year Saskatchewan had sustained losses in excess of 3.3 million acres of forestry land, a good portion of which is what is called the commercial zone where the province lost 815,892 acres, and the balance in the secondary zone where it lost 2,497,128 acres of forestry land in the fires. The province of Saskatchewan spent a total of $15 million to maintain a crew to fight the forest fires throughout the year.
In my question in the House I addressed myself in particular to the problem which arose close to my constituency. During the early part of the year and in the summer manoeuvres had taken place at the Canadian forces base Cold Lake. They were utilizing areas such as the Primrose Lake bombing range, part of which lies within the The Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency. During the manoeuvres in this part of Canada, two U.S. fighter aircraft crashed. One crashed within the bounds of the Primrose Lake bombing range and it has been positively identified as the cause of an extensive forest fire which burned much of the Primrose Lake bombing range and spread into the Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency.
Since the U.S. fighter aircraft has been identified as the cause of the forest fire in Saskatchewan, either the Department of National Defence or else the U.S. government have the responsibility to pay damages. I think that someone should reimburse those who have had losses as a result of the forest fire, thus setting a precedent following forest fires which are caused in this manner in years to come. I think there should be a cost recovery for extinguishing the fire to the provincial government and I think that lost revenues should be reimbursed to those who have sustained losses, such as the loggers, people involved in mining activities, in commercial fishing and in trapping, people who have lost much revenue in the inhabited areas which were burned. Thirdly, the province should be reimbursed for the revenue which it lost from taxing the beneficiaries in the areas which have been burned out.
I admit there is an agreement in existence between the province of Saskatchewan and the federal government with regard to the range. I am not particularly happy with that agreement but I have heard it stated that if there are losses within the range, the provincial government recovers some money for extinguishing the fire and it also receives some money for lost revenue, but nothing is provided either by the provincial government or the federal government to reimburse those people who have lost some benefits from logging, fishing or trapping. Outside the range nothing is provided by the federal government to benefit people who have suffered lost revenue from which the province of Saskatchewan would also benefit.
This evening I am asking the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, to consider the provision of some money to those people who have suffered losses as a result of the forest fire.
I think that payments to these people and to the provincial government for damages sustained outside the area to which 1 referred should be made either by the Department of National Defence or the U.S. government which should be held responsible for a fire which was caused by one of their fighter aircraft while on manoeuvres over Canada.
Before closing let me indicate that I would like to see the federal government-and I would like to hear its comments on this issue-develop a user plan for the Primrose Lake bombing range in the Saskatchewan sector whereby people can go into that area to conduct logging operations for part of the year or to harvest some of the fish or furs within the bombing range, so that the federal government, the provincial government and the people who actually wish to use the range can begin to co-operate. I am referring to places such as Canoe Narrows, Dillon, Buffalo Narrows, Pierceland, Goodsoil and many other communities. It would utilize some of the resources within the Primrose Lake bombing range which are of no benefit to anyone right now other than those involved in the military manoeuvres which take place there.
With those comments I would like to leave this matter. Although the parliamentary secretary might not be prepared to answer some of the points I have raised, I would like her to
January 12, 1981

write or contact me with information arising out of my comments this evening.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Ursula Appolloni (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-U.S. FIGHTER AIRCRAFT CRASHING ON CANADIAN SOIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member referred to the forest fires in Ontario. At this time 1 should like to pay sincere, albeit belated, congratulations to the members of our defence staff who did fantastic work in airlifting people out of the area most affected, particularly the Kenora-Rainy River area.
The two American aircraft which crashed in the area of the hon. member were participating in exercise Maple Flag, an operational exercise conducted semi-annually at Canadian Forces base in Cold Lake. The purpose of the exercise is to improve the operational capability of our fighter crews by providing realistic training in a simulated high threat environment.
Following each crash a comprehensive investigation was carried out. In each case, it was quickly determined by flight safety specialist officers that there was no requirement to ground other participating aircraft. Therefore, flying was continued with the restriction that because of the risk of forest fire no live ammunition would be expended.
The issue of fire protection and fire fighting is thoroughly covered in the agreement between the Government of Canada and the province of Saskatchewan which covers Canadian forces' use of the Saskatchewan portion of the Primrose Lake weapons range. A similar agreement exists with the government of Alberta for the Alberta portion of the range. These agreements have been in force since 1954.
Adjournment Debate
Under the terms of the agreement, the Government of Canada contributes six cents per acre, or approximately $85,000 annually, to the province of Saskatchewan to provide fire protection and fire fighting services. Additionally the Government of Canada agrees to pay one-half of costs in excess of $10,000 per year incurred by the government of Saskatchewan for fighting fires in the range area. The fires caused by the two accidents in question are covered under this agreement.
I should like to add that the minister formally replied to the hon. member's letter of November 28 on this subject and on other aspects of the utilization of the Primrose air weapons range. That letter was sent to the hon. member's office this morning.
We in Canada are fortunate to be able to offer to our NATO partners and friends some unique training facilities in terms of both topography and climate. It is very much a part of our contributions to the alliance and one that is very welcome by our allies.
Also I should like to remind the hon. member opposite that our own Canadian forces enjoy the hospitality of those friends and allies wherever and whenever they train, be it in Europe or in the United States, under similar reciprocal agreements.
